A large number of suspicious orders for second-hand books have led many booksellers to believe that these books were actually purchased on behalf of AI companies, allowing them to scan the contents and use the text as material for AI training — without the authors' knowledge and without any compensation.

An AirTag hidden inside a rare book among a bulk order eventually ended up at Amazon's AI training facility, seemingly confirming this theory…

Booksellers who specialise in second-hand books generally receive orders for single volumes or a few related titles. But for quite some time now, some booksellers have independently reported receiving large bulk orders for second-hand books, with no obvious connection between the titles on the lists.

Suspicion has fallen on the possibility that these books were being bought by AI companies, taken apart from their bindings, and run through high-speed scanning equipment to extract the text, which was then fed into AI systems as training material.

Doing so is done without the authors' consent and without paying any fee for the use of their work — which is, to put it bluntly, highly unethical — but until now there has been no solid evidence to prove it was really happening. An investigation by 404 Media appears to have changed that.

That report sits behind a paywall, but TNW relayed the findings, noting that the tracking device in question was an AirTag, and that staff at the facility confirmed what was being done there.

Second-hand books are particularly valuable because, for titles published after 2022, some of the content may itself have been written or edited by AI; in other words, using these books to train AI amounts to training one AI on the output of another. Publishing contracts will almost always expressly forbid authors from using AI-generated content, but there will always be people who ignore that rule. As for self-published books, there is effectively nothing that can be meaningfully policed.

Part of the problem is that intellectual property law has not yet caught up with this practice. In the UK, this kind of behaviour would very likely already be illegal, but in the US a 2025 ruling astonishingly found the practice to be lawful, calling it a "transformative" use of copyrighted works.
